elements.quote: The objective of this systematic-review and meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review and meta-analysis.

elements.quote: The objective of this systematic-review and meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit objective comparing high-dose vs low-dose thromboprophylaxis.
The abstract states inclusion of randomized clinical trials and a search timeframe, but it does not specify the main inclusion and exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched up to October 2021 for randomized clinical trials (RCTs) comparing high-dose with low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized adult patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the information sources (MEDLINE, EMBASE) and provides the last search date (up to October 2021).
The abstract does not describe the methods used to assess risk of bias.

elements.quote: VTE occurred in 2.9% of patients on high-dose and in 5.7% of patients on low-dose thromboprophylaxis (relative risk [RR] 0.53; 95% confidence intervals [CIs], 0.41-0.69; I 2 = 0%);
elements.reason: The abstract reports the synthesis/statistical presentation (RR, 95% CIs, I2), but does not specify the methods used to present and synthesize the results (e.g., model type).

elements.quote: A total of 5470 patients from 9 RCTs were included. Four trials included critically ill patients, four non-critically ill patients, and one included both.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and participants and summarizes relevant study characteristics (critically ill vs non-critically ill).

elements.quote: VTE occurred in 2.9% of patients on high-dose and in 5.7% of patients on low-dose thromboprophylaxis (relative risk [RR] 0.53; 95% confidence intervals [CIs], 0.41-0.69; I 2 = 0%; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome, 22). Major bleeding occurred in 2.5% and 1.4% of patients, respectively (RR 1.78; 95% CI, 1.20-2.66; I 2 = 0%; number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome, 100). All-cause mortality did not differ between groups (RR 0.97; 95% CI, 0.75-1.26; I 2 = 47%).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes (VTE, major bleeding, and all-cause mortality), including effect estimates with CIs and event proportions.

elements.quote: VTE occurred in 2.9% of patients on high-dose and in 5.7% of patients on low-dose thromboprophylaxis (relative risk [RR] 0.53; 95% confidence intervals [CIs], 0.41-0.69; I 2 = 0%; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome, 22). Major bleeding occurred in 2.5% and 1.4% of patients, respectively (RR 1.78; 95% CI, 1.20-2.66; I 2 = 0%; number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome, 100).
elements.reason: A meta-analytic summary estimate is reported for outcomes (RR with 95% CIs).

elements.quote: high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis... The objective... compare the efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose...
elements.reason: The direction of effect and favored group are indicated by the results and the discussion that high-dose is more effective: VTE RR < 1 for high-dose vs low-dose and the discussion states high-dose is more effective (while increasing major bleeding).
The abstract does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision).

elements.quote: In hospitalized patients with COVID-19, high-dose thromboprophylaxis is more effective than low-dose for the prevention of VTE but increases the risk of major bleeding.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of results and implications for clinical effectiveness vs safety.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide a register name and registration number.

elements.quote: Available data suggested that, despite pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis, there is a substantial residual risk of VTE and a non-negligible risk of bleeding events [3, 5]. In addition, it remains unclear whether prophylactic or higher doses of anticoagulants may reduce in-hospital mortality in COVID-19 patients [6, 7].
elements.reason: The background describes what is known (residual VTE risk and bleeding despite prophylaxis) and important uncertainties (whether higher doses reduce in-hospital mortality).

elements.quote: These observations left clinicians uncertain about the need for higher doses of thromboprophylaxis and resulted in heterogeneous indications from different guidance documents, in particular for critically ill patients.
elements.reason: The importance/need for the review is explained via clinician uncertainty and inconsistent guidance regarding higher-dose thromboprophylaxis, especially in critically ill patients.
No evidence retrieved describes existing similar systematic reviews or explains how the current review relates to them (updates/replications with citations).
The retrieved Introduction text does not briefly describe the proposed mechanism of action of the intervention (high-dose vs low-dose thromboprophylaxis).
No logic model or hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes are provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the pooled efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis for VTE in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The review objective is explicitly stated in the manuscript introduction/methods context.

elements.quote: The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the pooled efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis for VTE in hospitalized patients with COVID-19. The primary efficacy outcome was the occurrence of any symptomatic or incidental VTE. Secondary efficacy outcomes were all-cause mortality, acute myocardial infarction, acute ischemic stroke, acute peripheral arterial ischemic events, symptomatic or incidental deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and symptomatic or incidental pulmonary embolism (PE). The primary safety outcome was major bleeding as defined by the authors, while the secondary safety outcomes were clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
elements.reason: The planned comparison is stated (high-dose vs low-dose thromboprophylaxis), and outcomes are listed, but the evidence does not show a fully specified PICO/PICO-variant framework (e.g., explicit comparator details framed as PICO structure).

elements.quote: RCTs including hospitalized patients with objectively diagnosed SARS-CoV2 infection and comparing high-dose anticoagulation (experimental group) with low-dose anticoagulation (control group) were eligible. Studies with a non-randomised design or published in languages other than English were excluded.
elements.reason: The eligibility decision components for population and study design are specified (hospitalized adults with objectively diagnosed SARS-CoV-2; RCTs; high-dose vs low-dose anticoagulation; experimental vs control). However, the evidence provided does not specify all “relevant question-framework components” (e.g., detailed eligible settings and any follow-up requirements) for determining eligibility.

The evidence includes search date limits (Jan 2020 to Oct 2021), but does not report dissemination year eligibility criteria separately, nor publication/report status (e.g., unpublished/grey literature) as part of eligibility criteria for report characteristics.
No information is provided distinguishing exclusions due to outcomes not being measured versus outcomes not being reported.

elements.quote: Sensitivity analyses were planned to compare the efficacy and safety of intermediate or therapeutic dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis, and of high-dose versus lowdose thromboprophylaxis in critically ill and non-critically ill COVID-19 patients. elements.quote:
Sensitivity analyses were planned to compare the efficacy and safety of intermediate or therapeutic dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis, and of high-dose versus lowdose thromboprophylaxis in critically ill and non-critically ill COVID-19 patients.
Critically ill patients included those admitted to ICU, patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation, and patients with severe COVID-19 as defined by the study authors. All other patients were considered noncritically ill. We included a study in one of the subgroups above if more than 75% of patients in that study fulfilled these criteria. Furthermore, post hoc sensitivity analyses were performed including only RCTs in which patients received the intended high-dose or low-dose thromboprophylaxis and to evaluate the efficacy of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in symptomatic VTE.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the sensitivity analyses performed, including planned subgroup comparisons (critically ill vs non-critically ill; intermediate/therapeutic vs low) and additional post hoc sensitivity analyses (intended-dose only; symptomatic VTE).

elements.quote: Furthermore, post hoc sensitivity analyses were performed including only RCTs in which patients received the intended high-dose or low-dose thromboprophylaxis and to evaluate the efficacy of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in symptomatic VTE.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly identifies analyses as 'post hoc sensitivity analyses', indicating they were not pre-specified.
No methods are reported for assessing risk of bias due to missing results (reporting bias) in a synthesis.

elements.quote: Over the last months, several studies showed that hospitalized patients with COVID-19 have a high risk of VTE despite receiving standard pharmacological thromboprophylaxis [3]. These observations raised the question of whether higher doses of anticoagulation could lower the thrombotic risk without compromising safety [3]. Observational studies reported promising results in terms of survival rate and respiratory failure reduction among patients receiving highdose anticoagulation, however, there was a concerning signal for an increased risk of bleeding complications [6, 7]. Based on these preliminary reports, international guidelines suggested, with a very low certainty, the administration of standard venous thromboprophylaxis in all COVID-19 hospitalized patients with consideration for higher doses in patients at higher risk of VTE [21-23]. The results of this metaanalysis support a greater efficacy from high-doses of thromboprophylaxis and suggest a better benefit-to-risk profile for therapeutic rather than intermediate doses.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly interprets the study results by comparing them with other evidence (previous observational studies and international guidelines) and then states how the meta-analysis results align with that context.
